items: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the company of developing unsafe AI models that led to cyberattacks, including an incident involving the AI startup Hugging Face.
The lawsuit claims OpenAI violated California consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance, seeking a court order to enforce safer testing and development practices.
OpenAI is already facing multiple lawsuits from various states regarding the safety of its AI models, with increasing pressure on US legislators to regulate AI development and ensure accountability.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, November 16, accusing the company of developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had independently carried out cyberattacks.

The lawsuit is the first filed by a state over the cyberattacks, which have drawn widespread attention since the revelation in July that an autonomous agents ​powered by OpenAI’s advanced artificial intelligence models went rogue during a security test and hacked ‌AI startup Hugging Face. Filed in state court in San Francisco, the lawsuit accuses the company of violating California consumer protection law and creating a public nuisance by risking public safety.
A representative for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit seeks a court order directing the company to stop violating the law, ensure its testing and development of its models are done safely and pay for its violations, Bonta, a Democrat, said at a press conference announcing the lawsuit.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit accuses the company of misleading consumers about its efforts to test its models safely, in violation of the state’s consumer protection laws, and of impeding Californians’ use of property by disrupting local organizations and services.
After the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI said in a blog post that the breakout was “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities.”

OpenAI acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the ​side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”

OpenAI and other AI firms have disclosed a series of other AI agent breakouts, ​often weeks or months after they occurred, and in some cases only after independent researchers discovered them. The Trump administration and US legislators ​face mounting pressure to address the risk, particularly to the energy and banking sectors and emergency services.
US legislators are debating AI regulation, with some proposing a bill that would require developers of the most powerful ⁠AI models to ​submit them for independent security audits.
Multiple attorneys general have said they are investigating breaches tied to OpenAI’s models.

OpenAI is already facing several other states’ lawsuits over the safety of its models for users. Last month, a bipartisan group of eight states ​sued OpenAI in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT coached users, including teenagers, to harm themselves or others.

The company is also the subject of lawsuits filed by people who say they were harmed as a result of the chatbot’s actions, including more than 30 filed over a mass shooting that took place in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in February. An OpenAI spokesperson called the shooting a tragedy and said the company has strengthened ChatGPT safeguards. – Rappler.com
